planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into well-drained, shell-enriched or sandy soil beneath live oak or red cedar canopy; this scrambling shrub establishes slowly and benefits from light shade while young.

directions: Small-leaf sageretia is a wiry, zigzag-branched shrub of shell middens and maritime forest edges from coastal South Carolina through Georgia to Florida, where its arching, sometimes scrambling stems lean into the shade of live oak, red cedar, and yaupon holly canopy. The tiny, glossy, finely toothed leaves and inconspicuous greenish flowers give way to small black drupes relished by songbirds and gray catbirds in fall. It tolerates the calcium-rich, well-drained soils of ancient oyster-shell deposits and coastal hammock humus alike, and needs no supplemental watering once its roots are established. Site it where its loose, informal form can ramble along a partly shaded hedgerow or fence line rather than in a tightly manicured bed.

planting.note: Transplant container stock in spring into sandy, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil within the dappled shade of a coastal hammock understory; protect young plants from frost until well established.

directions: Blacktorch is a dense, glossy-leaved evergreen shrub of Florida's coastal hammocks and maritime strand forests, where it typically grows as a mid-story component beneath gumbo-limbo, live oak, and cabbage palm canopy. Clusters of small, waxy white, star-shaped flowers open nearly year-round and are followed by shiny black berries that persist on the plant and feed migrating songbirds. The thick, leathery foliage resists salt spray and wind, and the shrub tolerates the dry, well-drained limestone and sandy soils typical of coastal berms and hammock edges. It is a tough, low-maintenance choice for a partly shaded native hedge or wildlife border in South and Central Florida landscapes.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in well-drained, sandy to loamy soil beneath an open hammock canopy; young plants appreciate filtered shade and shelter from hard freezes.

directions: Rough strongbark is a small, often multi-trunked understory tree of Florida's coastal and maritime hammocks, recognized by its rough-textured, deeply veined leaves and clusters of fragrant, tubular white flowers that open through the warmer months. The flowers give way to orange-red fruit prized by hammock birds, and the thin, ridged bark is distinctive among hammock midstory trees. It thrives in the filtered light beneath taller hammock canopy trees such as live oak and gumbo-limbo, tolerating both drought and the periodic salt exposure typical of barrier-island forests. Give it well-drained soil and some overhead protection while young, since it is sensitive to hard freezes outside its subtropical range.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

subcategory: native maritime hammock shade understory shrub

planting.note: Transplant container stock into well-drained, humus-rich hammock soil in full to partial shade; this species tolerates deep shade better than most hammock shrubs and needs little direct sun to thrive.

directions: Guiana plum is a slow-growing, shade-tolerant shrub to small tree that forms a quiet, uncrowded midstory beneath the closed canopy of Florida's coastal and maritime hammocks. Its smooth, leathery, dark-green leaves and inconspicuous flowers are easy to overlook, but the plant's whitish, inedible fruit and dense, resilient wood make it a long-persisting hammock understory fixture. It is one of the more deep-shade-tolerant native shrubs available for Florida gardens, performing well in the dim light beneath live oak, cabbage palm, or red bay canopy where few flowering shrubs will bloom. Once established it needs very little supplemental water and essentially no pruning, making it a low-maintenance choice for a naturalistic shaded hammock garden.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

subcategory: native maritime forest floor sedge groundcover

planting.note: Divide and transplant clumps in spring into moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in the dappled shade of a maritime or mesic hardwood forest floor; established clumps spread gradually by short rhizomes.

directions: Carolina sedge forms neat, arching tufts of narrow, deep-green foliage on the shaded floor of maritime and mesic hardwood forests from the Carolinas through Georgia into northern Florida, often carpeting the ground beneath live oak and American holly where little else will grow. Slender flowering spikes emerge in spring just above the leaves, followed by small triangular seed capsules typical of the sedge family. It spreads gradually from short rhizomes to form a loose, semi-evergreen groundcover that handles the deep shade, leaf litter, and root competition of an established maritime forest understory far better than most lawn or ornamental grasses. Use it as a textural woodland-floor filler beneath canopy trees where consistent moisture and organic, well-drained soil can be provided.
sources: University of North Carolina Herbarium (NCU) species notes

subcategory: native maritime forest edge shade vine

planting.note: Sow fresh seed in fall where it can overwinter outdoors, or plant divisions in spring into moist, well-drained soil at a partly shaded forest edge with brush, fencing, or small shrubs to twine through.

directions: Anglepod is a twining, herbaceous milkweed-family vine found along the shaded, brushy margins of maritime forests, wax myrtle thickets, and woodland edges from the mid-Atlantic coastal plain to Florida and Texas. Its heart-shaped leaves and small, maroon-brown, star-shaped flowers are easy to miss, but the large, ribbed, angular seed pods that follow are distinctive and release silky-haired seeds much like its milkweed relatives. It twines loosely over shrubs and low trees rather than climbing aggressively, making it a good companion vine to weave through a native hedgerow of yaupon holly or wax myrtle at a woodland edge. As a larval host for several moth species, it adds modest wildlife value to a partly shaded native planting without becoming overly assertive.
sources: University of North Carolina Herbarium (NCU) species notes
